cards.def:
**A pair of equations — one linear, one quadratic — solved together.**
• A solution is any (x, y) pair that makes BOTH equations true at once.
• Graphically, the solutions are exactly where the line and the parabola intersect.
cards.hint: Solving the system means finding every point the line and the parabola share.

cards.def:
**A line and a parabola can intersect 0, 1, or 2 times — never more.**
• A straight line simply can't cross a U-shaped curve more than twice.
• Which of the three happens depends on exactly where the line sits relative to the parabola.
cards.hint: Picture a line sliding up and down past a parabola — it goes from missing it, to grazing it once, to slicing through it twice.

cards.def:
**The line crosses the parabola at two separate points.**
• This is the most common case for a line that isn't specially placed.
• Both intersection points are genuine solutions to the system.
cards.hint: Two solutions means the line genuinely cuts across the curve.

cards.def:
**The line touches the parabola at exactly one point without crossing through it — it's tangent to the curve.**
• This happens at exactly one specific position for a line of a given slope.
• Substituting and solving will produce a discriminant of 0, the same signal as a repeated root anywhere else.
cards.hint: Tangent means "just grazing" — the line touches but doesn't cut through.

cards.def:
**The line never touches the parabola at all.**
• Substituting the two equations together produces a quadratic with a negative discriminant.
• Graphically, the line passes entirely above (or below) the parabola.
cards.hint: No solution means the algebra will hand you a negative number under a square root.

cards.def:
**Substitute the linear equation's expression for y into the quadratic equation, then solve the resulting equation for x.**
• This turns two equations into one, in a single variable.
• Once you have each x-value, substitute back into the LINEAR equation (it's simpler) to find the matching y-value.
cards.hint: Solve for x first using substitution, then go back to the easier (linear) equation to find y.

cards.def:
**Substitute the (x, y) pair into BOTH original equations and confirm each one is true.**
• A pair that only satisfies one equation isn't a solution to the system.
• This catches arithmetic errors made anywhere earlier in the process.
cards.hint: A real solution has to satisfy both equations — checking just one isn't enough.

cards.term: Application: where a path meets a boundary
cards.def:
**A thrown object's path (quadratic) and the ground or a hillside (linear) form a linear-quadratic system — the solution is where the object lands.**
• Setting the two equations equal and solving for x gives the horizontal distance traveled.
• Only the solution matching the real-world direction of travel is kept — often the positive one.
cards.hint: The object's flight ends exactly where its path equation and the ground equation agree.

cards.def:
**For y = x² − 4 and y = x + 2: substituting gives x² − 4 = x + 2, so x² − x − 6 = 0, factoring to x = −2 or x = 3.**
• At x = −2: y = −2 + 2 = 0, giving the point (−2, 0).
• At x = 3: y = 3 + 2 = 5, giving the point (3, 5).
cards.hint: Once you know x, plug it into the LINEAR equation — it's always less arithmetic than the quadratic one.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of times a line and a parabola can intersect?
questions.hint: Picture the shapes — how many times can a straight line cross a single U-curve?
steps: A parabola is a single smooth curve that only bends one direction.
A straight line can cross it as it goes up, and again as it comes back down — but never a third time.
So the maximum number of intersection points is two.

ex.main: **Two.** A straight line simply cannot cross a parabola's single curve more than twice.

questions.q: A line is tangent to a parabola. How many solutions does the linear-quadratic system have?
opts: It depends on the parabola's direction
questions.hint: Tangent means the line just touches the curve, without crossing through it.
steps: "Tangent" describes a line that touches a curve at exactly one point, without passing through to the other side.
That single point of contact is the system's only solution.
So a tangent line means exactly one solution.

ex.main: **One.** Tangent is the exact boundary case between two solutions and zero — it touches, but doesn't cross.

questions.q: What are the solutions of the system y = x² − 4 and y = x + 2?
questions.hint: Substitute the linear expression for y into the quadratic equation.
steps: Substitute x + 2 for y in the quadratic equation: x² − 4 = x + 2.
Rearrange to standard form: x² − x − 6 = 0, which factors as (x − 3)(x + 2) = 0, giving x = 3 or x = −2.
Substitute each x back into the linear equation y = x + 2: x = 3 gives y = 5, and x = −2 gives y = 0. The solutions are (3, 5) and (−2, 0).

ex.main: **(−2, 0) and (3, 5).** Substituting back into the LINEAR equation for y is always the easier arithmetic of the two options.

questions.q: What is the solution of the system y = x² − 4x + 7 and y = 2x − 2?
questions.hint: After substituting, check whether the resulting equation has one solution or two.
steps: Substitute 2x − 2 for y: x² − 4x + 7 = 2x − 2, which rearranges to x² − 6x + 9 = 0.
This factors as (x − 3)² = 0, so x = 3 is the only solution — this line is tangent to the parabola.
Substitute x = 3 into y = 2x − 2: y = 6 − 2 = 4. The single solution is (3, 4).

ex.main: **(3, 4).** The repeated root (x − 3)² = 0 is exactly what a tangent line produces algebraically — a discriminant of 0.

questions.q: Does the system y = x² + 3 and y = x − 5 have any real solutions?
opts: No — substituting produces a negative discriminant
Yes — there is exactly one solution
No — a line and a parabola never intersect
questions.hint: Substitute, rearrange to standard form, and check the discriminant.
steps: Substitute x − 5 for y: x² + 3 = x − 5, which rearranges to x² − x + 8 = 0.
Compute the discriminant: (−1)² − 4(1)(8) = 1 − 32 = −31.
The discriminant is negative, so there are no real solutions — this line never meets this parabola.

ex.main: **No — the discriminant is negative.** A negative discriminant here means the same thing it always does: no real solutions, so the line passes entirely above or below the curve.

questions.q: A ball's path is modeled by y = −0.5x² + 6x, where x is horizontal distance in feet and y is height in feet. The ground is y = 0. How far does the ball travel before it lands?
questions.hint: Set the two equations equal and solve — one solution will be where the ball starts.
steps: Set the path equal to the ground: −0.5x² + 6x = 0.
Factor: x(−0.5x + 6) = 0, giving x = 0 or x = 12.
x = 0 is where the ball is thrown from; x = 12 is where it lands. The ball travels 12 feet.

ex.main: **12 feet.** One solution is always the throwing point itself (x = 0) in a problem like this — the OTHER solution is the one that actually answers the question.

questions.q: A ball's path is y = −0.5x² + 6x, and a hillside is modeled by y = x (both in feet). Where does the ball land on the hillside?
questions.hint: Set the two equations equal, solve for x, then use either equation to find y.
steps: Set the equations equal: −0.5x² + 6x = x.
Rearrange: −0.5x² + 5x = 0, then factor: x(−0.5x + 5) = 0, giving x = 0 or x = 10.
x = 0 is the launch point; x = 10 is where it lands on the hillside. Substituting into y = x gives y = 10, so the landing point is (10, 10).

ex.main: **(10, 10).** The hillside being a line through the origin, y = x, is why the landing point's x and y coordinates come out equal.

questions.q: What is the first step in solving a linear-quadratic system by substitution?
opts: Substitute the linear equation's expression for y into the quadratic equation
Substitute the quadratic equation into itself
questions.hint: You're trying to turn two equations into one.
steps: The goal of substitution is to combine two equations into a single equation in one variable.
Since the linear equation is simpler, its expression for y gets substituted into the quadratic equation.
This produces one quadratic equation in x alone, which can then be solved normally.

ex.main: **Substitute the linear equation's expression for y into the quadratic equation.** The simpler equation always does the substituting; the more complex one receives it.

questions.q: Dyani solves the system y = 2x² − 6x + 4 and x − y = 7 by writing x + 2x² − 6x + 4 = 7 as her first step. What is her error?
opts: She should have solved x − y = 7 for y first, getting y = x − 7, and substituted THAT — not x itself
There is no error — her equation is correct
She should have substituted the quadratic equation into the linear one instead
She needed to substitute for x, not for y
questions.hint: Look carefully at what x − y = 7 actually says about y before anything gets substituted.
steps: The second equation is x − y = 7, which needs to be solved for y first: y = x − 7.
Dyani instead substituted x itself in place of y, which isn't what the equation says.
The correct substitution is 2x² − 6x + 4 = x − 7, not x + 2x² − 6x + 4 = 7.

ex.main: **She substituted x for y instead of solving for y first.** x − y = 7 isn't already solved for y — that has to happen before substitution, the same as any other linear equation.

questions.q: A system's equations, when substituted together, simplify to x² + 4 = 0. What does this tell you about the system?
opts: The line and parabola have no real intersection points
The line and parabola intersect at exactly one point
The line and parabola intersect at (0, 4)
There's a mistake, since this can't happen
questions.hint: Think about what kind of solutions x² + 4 = 0 actually has.
steps: Solving x² + 4 = 0 gives x² = −4, which has no real solutions — only the complex solutions x = ±2i.
No real x-values mean no real points where the line and the parabola meet.
So this result tells you the system has no real solutions — the line never touches this parabola.

ex.main: **No real intersection points.** A quadratic that simplifies to something with no real roots is a completely valid, meaningful result — it's telling you the graphs simply don't meet.

questions.q: What does a solution to a linear-quadratic system represent graphically?
opts: A point where the line and the parabola intersect
The slope of the line at that point
questions.hint: A solution has to satisfy both equations — where does that happen visually?
steps: A solution (x, y) makes both the linear equation and the quadratic equation true at the same time.
On a graph, a point that lies on both curves is exactly where those two curves cross or touch.
So a solution represents a point where the line and the parabola intersect.

ex.main: **A point where the line and the parabola intersect.**

questions.q: What are the solutions of the system y = 3x² and y = −3x²?
questions.hint: Both equations here are quadratic, not one linear and one quadratic — solve the same way regardless.
steps: Set the two expressions equal: 3x² = −3x².
Add 3x² to both sides: 6x² = 0, so x² = 0, meaning x = 0.
Substitute back: y = 3(0)² = 0. The only solution is (0, 0).

ex.main: **(0, 0) only.** Both parabolas share only their vertex — one opens upward, the other downward, from the exact same point.

questions.q: A system's substitution produces the equation x² − 8x + 16 = 0. How many solutions does the linear-quadratic system have, and why?
opts: One — the equation factors as (x − 4)², a repeated root
Two — every quadratic equation has two solutions
Zero — the equation doesn't factor with integers
One — because the coefficient of x² is 1
questions.hint: Factor the equation and see whether the two solutions turn out to be the same value.
steps: Factor x² − 8x + 16: this is a perfect square trinomial, (x − 4)².
Setting it to 0 gives x − 4 = 0 twice — a repeated root, so x = 4 is the only distinct solution.
This means the line is tangent to the parabola, giving exactly one solution to the system.

ex.main: **One.** A repeated root — the same value showing up twice in the factoring — always means the line just grazes the parabola rather than crossing it.

questions.q: Why must you check a candidate solution in BOTH of the original equations, not just one?
opts: A pair satisfying only one equation isn't a true solution to the system
Checking one equation is always sufficient
The linear equation is never worth checking
The quadratic equation is always the one with errors
questions.hint: Think about what it actually means for a point to solve a SYSTEM, rather than a single equation.
steps: A solution to a system has to make every equation in that system true — not just one of them.
A point could satisfy the linear equation by coincidence while not lying on the parabola at all, or vice versa.
So checking only one equation could let a false solution slip through — both must be verified.

ex.main: **A pair satisfying only one equation isn't a true solution to the system.** "Solving the system" means satisfying every equation in it, simultaneously — that's the definition, not just good practice.

questions.q: Azzure and William both want to solve the system y = 2x² − 4x + 9 and y − 1 = 3x without graphing. Azzure substitutes 2x² − 4x + 9 in place of y directly into the second equation. William first rewrites y − 1 = 3x as y = 3x + 1, then sets that equal to the quadratic. Whose approach is correct?
opts: William's — the second equation has to be solved for y before substituting, and Azzure skipped that step
Azzure's — substituting directly is always valid, regardless of the equation's form
Both are correct and will get the same answer either way
Neither is correct — the equations must be added instead of substituted
questions.hint: Check whether y − 1 = 3x is already solved for y.
steps: Substitution requires knowing exactly what y equals, so the equation needs y isolated on one side first.
y − 1 = 3x is not yet solved for y — William correctly rewrites it as y = 3x + 1 before substituting.
Azzure substitutes the quadratic expression into an equation that still has y − 1 on the left, which sets up the wrong equation entirely.

ex.main: **William's approach.** Substitution only works correctly once the equation you're substituting INTO has the shared variable fully isolated.

questions.q: What are the solutions of y = x² and y = 5x − 6?
questions.hint: Substitute and factor the resulting quadratic.
steps: Substitute x² for y: x² = 5x − 6, which rearranges to x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
Factor: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, giving x = 2 or x = 3.
Substitute back into y = x²: x = 2 gives y = 4, and x = 3 gives y = 9. The solutions are (2, 4) and (3, 9).

questions.q: A system has a line y = mx + b and a parabola y = x². For which value of b (with m fixed at 4) will the system have exactly one solution?
questions.hint: Set the equations equal, then find the value of b that makes the discriminant 0.
steps: Substitute: x² = 4x + b, which rearranges to x² − 4x − b = 0.
For one solution, the discriminant must be 0: (−4)² − 4(1)(−b) = 0, so 16 + 4b = 0.
Solve: 4b = −16, so b = −4.

ex.main: **b = −4.** Working backward from "exactly one solution" to the discriminant, then to the unknown coefficient, is the same move used with any quadratic — the fact that it started as a system doesn't change it.

questions.q: A line passes far above a downward-opening parabola's vertex and never comes near the curve. How many real solutions does this linear-quadratic system have?
questions.hint: If the graphs never meet, there's nothing for a solution to describe.
steps: A solution to the system requires a shared point between the line and the parabola.
If the line passes entirely above the parabola without ever touching it, no such shared point exists.
So the system has zero real solutions.

ex.main: **Zero.** No shared point on the graphs means no (x, y) pair can satisfy both equations at once.

questions.q: What are the solutions of the system y = −x² + 6x and y = 2x?
questions.hint: Substitute, rearrange, and factor out the common x.
steps: Substitute 2x for y: −x² + 6x = 2x, which rearranges to −x² + 4x = 0.
Factor out −x: −x(x − 4) = 0, giving x = 0 or x = 4.
Substitute into y = 2x: x = 0 gives y = 0, and x = 4 gives y = 8. The solutions are (0, 0) and (4, 8).

questions.q: Chris graphed the system y = −x² and y = 2x + b for several values of b and concluded the system could have either one or zero solutions, but never two. What did Chris overlook?
opts: For some values of b, the line crosses the downward parabola at two separate points
The system can never have exactly one solution, only zero or two
Chris used the wrong parabola — this one can never intersect a line at all
There is no error — Chris's conclusion is correct for a downward-opening parabola
questions.hint: Think about a line positioned to cross through the middle of a downward-opening parabola.
steps: A downward-opening parabola behaves the same way as an upward-opening one for this purpose — a line can still cross it, touch it once, or miss it entirely.

For a line positioned to pass through the parabola's interior (below its vertex, roughly), it will cross at two separate points — for example, y = 2x + b with b chosen so the line cuts through both branches.
So Chris's conclusion is incomplete: two solutions is still possible, just for a different range of b than he may have tested.

ex.main: **Two solutions is still possible — Chris likely just didn't test a value of b that put the line through the parabola's interior.** The direction a parabola opens changes nothing about the 0-1-2 rule; it only changes WHICH line positions produce each case.
